past_actions.summary: Host the monthly Auto Row worker appreciation lunch — discounted daily special for all shop employees. Put a handwritten chalkboard sign out front. Spend time at the counter talking with regulars, learning names of the newer hires.
past_actions.emotional_state: Content and purposeful. Mild background satisfaction from a strong lunch service. No anxiety. The inbox confirmation that things are stable reinforces what I already knew — no need to worry, just work.

past_actions.summary: Spend extended time on the floor during lunch service actively listening to what the Auto Row workers know and believe about the RoboRide timeline, the Phase 2 rollout, and what the bosses are saying. Ask careful, genuine questions — not as market research but as a neighbor who wants to understand. Record notes in the back after close.
past_actions.emotional_state: Frightened but functional. The fear is specific and real — not the ambient low-level dread of a bad week but a concrete threat that arrived with a timeline attached. There is grief underneath the fear, the grief of someone who has built something for thirty years watching the ground under it shift. She is not panicking. She is also not pretending. She refilled coffee cups she didn't need to refill. That is the honest measure of where she is.

past_actions.summary: Apply for Maria Santos's $5,000 small business stabilization grant. Fill out the paperwork this week. The qualification criteria are met. The money is not for spending — it is for extending runway if the 60% drop scenario materializes. A $5,000 cushion converts a 6.4-month runway into something closer to 7.5 months at 60% revenue loss. That is the difference between having time to adapt and not having time.
past_actions.emotional_state: Purposeful and cautious. The fear has not gone away but it has found a shape — it is no longer ambient, it is directional. There is something that feels like relief in deciding to act rather than continuing to observe. She is not confident. She is willing. That is not the same thing, but it is what the moment calls for.

past_actions.summary: Prepare and deliver testimony to Maria Santos's small business task force meeting. Document the concrete changes I've observed at the diner since the spending index began falling: reduced average check size, fewer covers per lunch shift, regulars substituting coffee-only visits for full meals. Bring three months of rough receipt tallies. Speak plainly about what a spending index of 73 feels like from behind a counter. Advocate for grant extension and expedited disbursement for pending applicants like myself.

Follow up directly with Maria Santos's office on the pending grant application submitted at tick 2. Call or visit in person. Ask for a status update and a realistic timeline. If expedited disbursement was discussed at the task force meeting, ask whether my application qualifies. The purpose is twofold: get information I need to plan, and remind them I exist and am waiting.

Contact RoboRide local partnership coordinator to inquire about the diner kitchen participating in the new delivery network. Betty calls the number listed in the partnership announcement and asks direct questions: what are the requirements to become a delivery prep partner, what does the revenue share look like, how quickly can a small kitchen get set up. She is not committing — she is gathering information so she can decide whether this is a real option or a dead end.

reflections.reflection: Six ticks in and I am looking at a spending index of 48, an unemployment rate climbing past 23%, and a savings account that just lost $4,268 in a single month. The diner is technically still open but 'employed' no longer describes what I am. The grant application I filed four ticks ago has not come through. Following up with Maria Santos's office cost me a month of savings and my employment classification. I do not fully understand why, but I know what it means: the system is not going to catch me gently. I have been operating in denial — not the weeping kind but the quiet kind, the kind that keeps you moving through familiar motions while the math gets worse. The spending index at 48 is the number that finally broke through. That is not a slow quarter. That is a structural change. I have to start treating it as one.
reflections.identity_shift: I came into this as the anchor. Thirty years at that counter meant I was the one who stayed while others came and went. That identity is under pressure now. I am not the anchor if the harbor empties out. I am starting to think of myself less as 'owner of the Auto Row Diner' and more as 'someone with a commercial kitchen, a location, and a food service skill set that could be deployed differently.' That shift is small and it hurts. But it is more honest than what I was holding onto.
regrets: I did not start the contingency math sooner. I was waiting for permission — a bad grant outcome, a specific revenue number, something official — before I would let myself seriously plan for a different scenario. That cost me time I did not have to waste.

I have not talked to Carlos Ruiz yet. He is pivoting — I can tell from the word-of-mouth — and he understands this neighborhood's mechanics better than almost anyone. I should have bought him lunch two ticks ago.
successes: I applied for the grant at tick 2 and I showed up at the task force meeting at tick 4. Neither of those things has paid off yet but they were the right calls. I was in the room. I am on record. That matters.

I am still here. The diner is still open. Savings are down but not gone. I have not made any panicked decisions — no fire sales, no dramatic pivots I cannot sustain. The caution that sometimes looks like denial has also kept me from making things worse.
reflections.adaptation_notes: The meeting with Stephanie Morris is the right next move — not because I trust her entirely but because she is looking at this market from the outside and I need that view. I have to get comfortable hearing information I do not want to hear. I also need to do the triage math privately: what does it cost to stay open at 40% revenue, to temporarily close, to sublet the kitchen, to convert part of the space. Not deciding — knowing. The difference between having options and being out of runway is whether I do that math now or later. I am doing it now.
